misconceptions.statement: Pulses and vegetables are the same food group.
misconceptions.why: Dal is cooked like a sabzi and both are eaten with roti, so they seem alike.
misconceptions.fix: Pulses (dals, beans) are rich in protein and belong with protein foods, while vegetables mainly give vitamins, minerals and fibre.

probe.question: Which group gives more protein: dal or lauki?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are the same group so they give the same protein.

misconceptions.root_belief: things used together belong to the same category

misconceptions.statement: Potato is a vegetable that counts the same as green leafy vegetables.
misconceptions.why: Potato is sold and cooked as a vegetable.
misconceptions.fix: Potato is mostly starch and acts like a cereal for energy, while green leafy vegetables give iron, vitamins and fibre.

probe.question: Is aloo sabzi enough for the vegetable part of the plate?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, potato is a vegetable so it fully covers it.

misconceptions.root_belief: a common name decides what something is

misconceptions.statement: If I eat plenty of one very healthy food, I do not need other foods.
misconceptions.why: Advertisements and 'superfoods' promote single foods as complete.
misconceptions.fix: No single food gives all nutrients, so we need a variety of foods from different groups each day.

probe.question: Is eating only milk and bananas daily enough for a child?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are very healthy so nothing else is needed.

misconceptions.statement: Carbohydrates like rice and roti are only for fattening, so athletes and growing children should avoid them.
misconceptions.why: Diet-culture messages and low-carb trends make students see carbohydrates as a weight-gain nutrient rather than the body's main fuel.
misconceptions.fix: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy, and the brain and muscles depend on them. Government of India dietary guidelines (ICMR-NIN) say cereals and millets should supply a large share of daily energy. Weight gain comes from eating more energy than you use, not from carbohydrates alone.

probe.question: A cricketer plays for 3 hours daily. Should he cut out rice and roti to stay fit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, rice and roti only make you fat, so he should stop eating them.

misconceptions.root_belief: Carbohydrates are inherently fattening and unhealthy

misconceptions.statement: Proteins are needed only by bodybuilders and athletes, so ordinary children do not need extra protein foods.
misconceptions.why: Protein powders and gym advertising link protein with muscles and exercise, so students think it is not for everyday growth.
misconceptions.fix: Everyone needs protein to grow, repair tissues, make enzymes and fight infection. Growing children and adolescents need it every day. Dal, milk, eggs and pulses provide it. Special supplements are not needed for most people.

probe.question: Does a 10-year-old who does not go to the gym need protein in their food?
probe.wrong_answer: No, protein is only for people who build muscles in a gym.

misconceptions.root_belief: Nutrients matter only for special groups, not everyone
misconceptions.source_hint: ICMR-NIN guidelines; WHO healthy diet fact sheet

misconceptions.statement: Eating any fat or oil makes you fat, so the healthiest diet has no fat at all.
misconceptions.why: The word 'fat' is confused with body fat, and advertisements for fat-free products reinforce this idea.
misconceptions.fix: The body needs a small amount of fat for energy, for absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K, and for cell health. WHO advises that fat should be limited and unsaturated fats preferred, not removed completely.

probe.question: If a child eats food cooked with no oil at all for a year, will they be healthier?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because fat is what makes people fat, so no oil is the healthiest.

misconceptions.root_belief: Dietary fat equals body fat, so avoid completely

misconceptions.statement: Vitamins and minerals give us energy, so a vitamin tablet can replace a meal.
misconceptions.why: Tonics and supplements are advertised as 'energy boosters', so students treat vitamins as fuel.
misconceptions.fix: Vitamins and minerals do not provide energy; they help the body work and protect it from disease. Energy comes from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Supplements cannot replace food, which also gives energy, protein and fibre.

probe.question: A student skips lunch and takes a multivitamin tablet instead. Will they get the energy they need?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, vitamins give energy, so the tablet is as good as a meal.

misconceptions.root_belief: Vitamins and supplements are sources of energy

misconceptions.statement: Fibre is useless because the body cannot digest it, so peeled and refined foods are better.
misconceptions.why: Students hear that fibre is 'not digested' and conclude that it is waste with no function.
misconceptions.fix: Fibre gives no energy but keeps the gut moving, prevents constipation and helps control blood sugar. WHO recommends eating whole grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses to get enough fibre.

probe.question: Is it better to peel all vegetables and fruits and throw away the roughage?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, roughage is not digested so it is of no use and should be removed.

misconceptions.root_belief: Indigestible means useless to the body
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Science textbook; WHO healthy diet fact sheet

misconceptions.statement: Vegetarians cannot get enough protein without eating eggs or meat.
misconceptions.why: Eggs and meat are shown as the main protein foods, so students believe plant foods have little or poor protein.
misconceptions.fix: Pulses, dals, soya, nuts and milk products provide protein. Eating dal with roti or rice together gives a good mix of amino acids, so a vegetarian diet can meet protein needs. This is an established point in Indian dietary guidelines.

probe.question: Can a vegetarian child who eats dal, roti, rice and curd get enough protein?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only eggs and meat give enough protein, so they will be short of protein.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only animal foods can supply enough protein

misconceptions.statement: White polished rice and maida are healthier than brown rice and whole wheat atta because they are cleaner and finer.
misconceptions.why: Students link whiteness and fine texture with purity and quality, and refined foods look more attractive.
misconceptions.fix: Polishing and refining remove the bran and germ, which hold fibre, B vitamins and minerals. Whole grains keep these nutrients. Government dietary guidelines recommend whole grains over refined ones.

probe.question: Which gives more nutrients: whole wheat atta or maida?
probe.wrong_answer: Maida, because it is finer and cleaner, so it is more nutritious.

misconceptions.root_belief: Refined or processed foods are purer, hence healthier

misconceptions.statement: Only eating fatty or oily food makes you gain weight; eating extra rice, roti or sweets does not.
misconceptions.why: Students connect the word 'fat' with fatty foods only and forget that extra carbohydrate energy is also stored.
misconceptions.fix: Any food eaten in excess of the body's energy needs, whether carbohydrate, fat or protein, is stored as body fat. WHO says weight gain comes from an energy imbalance: more energy taken in than used.

probe.question: A boy eats no oily food but takes extra helpings of rice and sweets every day and does little activity. Will he gain weight?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because he is not eating fat, so nothing can be stored as fat.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only fatty food causes body fat gain
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO obesity and overweight fact sheet

misconceptions.statement: A balanced diet is the same amount and type of food for everyone, whatever their age or work.
misconceptions.why: Students see one food plate chart in books and assume it gives a single fixed diet for all people.
misconceptions.fix: The amount of food needed depends on age, sex, body size and activity. A growing teenager, a pregnant woman and a farm labourer need more energy and certain nutrients than an inactive adult. The food groups stay the same but quantities change.

probe.question: Should a child who plays sports daily and an office worker who sits all day eat exactly the same quantity of food?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a balanced diet is the same for everybody.

misconceptions.statement: Millets are poor people's grains and have less nutrition than rice and wheat.
misconceptions.why: Millets were historically seen as low-status food and replaced by polished rice and wheat, so students assume they are lower quality.
misconceptions.fix: Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are rich in fibre, iron, calcium and other minerals, and often have more of these than polished rice. The Government of India promoted millets as 'Shree Anna' and the UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets.

probe.question: Which has more calcium: ragi or polished white rice?
probe.wrong_answer: White rice, because millets are only a poor man's food with little nutrition.

misconceptions.root_belief: Traditional low-status foods are nutritionally inferior
misconceptions.source_hint: Government of India Shree Anna / ICMR-NIN
